title: A boolean is not a word
idea: True is the boolean, but "True" in quotes is just text. They look alike but behave differently. Telling them apart is important.

exercises.prompt: Which one is a boolean (a yes/no value)?
exercises.explanation: True with no quotes is the boolean. "True" in quotes is just text that reads 'True'.
"False" in quotes is text. Without quotes, False is the boolean value.

exercises.prompt: True (no quotes) and "True" (with quotes) are the same thing.
exercises.explanation: They are different. True is a boolean; "True" is a string of letters. They just look similar when printed.
It prints the text False. Even though it reads the same, it's a string here, not the boolean.

exercises.prompt: Which prints the actual boolean, not text?
exercises.explanation: print(True) prints the boolean. The others all print text inside quotes.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece of code to what kind of value it is.
exercises.explanation: No quotes and capitalized = boolean. Quotes = text. Digits = number. The type decides how Python treats it.

exercises.prompt: Putting quotes around True turns it into text, not a yes/no value.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Quotes always mean 'this is text'. "True" is just the letters T-r-u-e.

exercises.prompt: You want a real yes/no value meaning 'no'. Which do you write?
exercises.explanation: The boolean for 'no' is False with no quotes. "False" would just be text.

exercises.prompt:
Both lines run:

print(True)
print("True")

What appears on screen?
exercises.explanation: Both print the text 'True' on screen - but the first is a boolean and the second is a string. On screen they look identical.

exercises.prompt: Why does it matter whether something is the boolean True or the text "True"?
options: Because the computer treats yes/no values and text differently
It does not matter at all
exercises.explanation: Soon we'll make decisions from booleans. A yes/no value and a piece of text are not interchangeable to the computer.
